Sequences

Sequences in Python are ordered, iterable collections of items. They are data structures.

Maintain the order in which elements are added
Zero-based indexing
Allow access to individual items by index numbers and slicing

There are several built-in sequence types that have specific characteristics and uses (do learn what the sequences are and how they differ)

Sequences are part of a larger discussion of type
All sequences are iterables, but not all iterables are sequences (later)

Default Execution Order in Python

At its simplest, Python code works in the following way

Top to bottom: Python reads and executes code line by line
Left to right (within a code line): Python evaluates expressions from left to right, following operator precedence.

Restated: in a simple .py script, Python follows a strict “top to bottom, left to right” execution order.
This strict execution order can be changed when we introduce control flow statements (if, for, while, match, etc.) or functions which have the ability to modify the execution order.

Objects (more later)

Everything in Python is an object – numbers, strings, lists, tuples, and functions, these are all objects.
Conceptually, an object is like a container or a box with a label on it.
Python is at heart an object oriented language but it supports multiple programming models (OOP, Procedural, and Functional)

(note) R is a functional programming language at heart

Every object is created from some class (more later). A class is a set of instructions or a template for creating objects.
Objects have a type and they also have attributes and methods (functions specific to that object).
The object oriented nature of Python makes the language very flexible.
But also a little tricky coming from R as Python at heart has a very different programming model.

Rules for Variable Names

They can only consist of:

Lowercase letters (a through z)

Uppercase letters (A through Z)

Digits (0 through 9)

The Underscore (_)

They are case-sensitive
They can begin with a letter or an underscore but not a digit.
They cannot be one of Python’s reserved keywords.

Code
 def factorial(n):
    """
    Calculates the factorial of a number.

    Args:
        n (int): The number to compute factorial for.

    Returns:
        int: The factorial of the number.
    """
    
    # This function calculates the factorial of a number using iteration.
    # It starts with a base value of 1 and multiplies by each number 
    # from 1 to n to get the final result.
    # If n is negative, it returns None.
    
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Please choose a non-negative number") # this will stop the function

    result = 1  # covers 0 and 1
    for i in range(2, n + 1): 
        result *= i  # Multiply result by i in each step

    return result

# Let's test it
# factorial(-1)

print(f"The factorial of 1 is: {factorial(1)} \n")

(extra) Last slide, practice reading some Python
Just for fun and practice see if you can figure out what is happening here. If you want to see if you were correct, see and try running the original script (find it here): https://ucla.box.com/s/hy7bsxaqj4lw17a51jyp5b777o7xim09


Code
#!/usr/bin/env python3


## Importing two functions from two libraries
from pathlib import Path
from pytubefix import YouTube

## Ask for a YouTube URL, input() is a built-in function
MY_URL = input('What is the URL of your YouTube video? ')
MY_PATH = Path.cwd()  # will save to the current working directory

## Create the custom function "get_filename" to allow the use to input their own name 
def get_filename(default=None):
    """Prompt the user for a filename with no extension"""
    while True:
        user_input = input("Enter a new name for the saved file (without extension) or press enter for its default name: ").strip() # removes whitespace
        if user_input == '':  # User pressed Enter without input
            return default
        elif Path(user_input).suffix.lower() != '.mp4':  
            user_input +=  '.mp4'
        return user_input

## Go out and get a video
yt = YouTube(MY_URL, 'WEB') # need 'WEB' or something comparable
ys = yt.streams.get_highest_resolution()

## use the get_filename() we wrote for this script
video_filename = get_filename()

## download the video
ys.download(output_path = MY_PATH, filename = video_filename, skip_existing = False)

Title IX Resources
UCLA prohibits gender discrimination, including sexual harassment, domestic and dating violence, sexual assault, and stalking. If you have experienced sexual harassment or sexual violence, there are a variety of resources to assist you.

CONFIDENTIAL RESOURCES: You can receive confidential support and advocacy at the CARE Advocacy Office for Sexual and Gender-Based Violence, 1st Floor Wooden Center West, (310) 206-2465. Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) also provides confidential counseling to all students and can be reached 24/7 at (310) 825-0768.
NON-CONFIDENTIAL RESOURCES: You can also report sexual violence or sexual harassment directly to the University’s Title IX Coordinator, 2241 Murphy Hall, titleix@conet.ucla.edu, (310) 206-3417. Reports to law enforcement can be made to UCPD at (310) 825-1491. These offices may be required to pursue an official investigation.
